title: Give Your Children Shakespeare
author: Jenna A. Robinson
summary: Jenna A. Robinson reviews Ken Ludwig's How to Teach Your Children Shakespeare and recommends it to parents who want to restore memorization and the Western canon to their children's education. The review rests on Ludwig's claim that children's brains are built for memorization and that Shakespeare, as one of the two bedrocks of Western civilization in English, is the best material to fill that capacity. Ludwig's method pairs 26 passages for memorizing with play summaries, modern translations of hard lines and short scholarly background. Robinson praises the book for plunging straight into a beautiful, easy passage so that even hesitant readers see the method working. She also names its limits: it is not a standalone book, it assumes the plays are read in full, and it omits the sonnets, which would suit memorization well. Her bottom line is that very little Shakespeare is taught in schools today, so parents should take up the work themselves.
points: Ludwig's central claim is that memorization is the route to truly knowing Shakespeare, and that it works only if the child understands every word being memorized.
The book treats Shakespeare as a cultural bedrock, arguing that Hamlet, Macbeth, Juliet and Ophelia now sit alongside the biblical figures as archetypes of Western consciousness.
Starting with one vivid, easily memorized passage in the first chapter lowers the barrier for parents and children who feel intimidated by the Bard.
Robinson's caveats are practical: read each play in full first, and extend Ludwig's method to the sonnets he leaves out.
The review frames home memorization as a remedy for schools that teach very little Shakespeare, which makes it a parent-led act of cultural recovery.
quotes: Children’s brains are designed for memorization. Almost without trying, they absorb whatever they hear and see—from Taylor Swift to sports statistics.
Ludwig’s goal throughout How to Teach Your Children Shakespeare is to “demystify” the Bard, whom he calls “one of the two great bedrocks of Western civilization in English.
But truly knowing Shakespeare requires memorization. “In order to memorize something…you have to work slowly, and you have to understand every word of what you’re memorizing.

By plunging straight into one of Shakespeare’s most beautiful,and easy-to-memorize images, Ludwig captures the reader’s imagination. His clear instructions convince even the most hesitant reader that this method works.
More importantly, Ludwig omits Shakespeare’s 154 sonnets, many of which would make excellent choices for memorization.
Although we may not realize it, his work has profoundly shaped our language and even the way we think.
Very little Shakespeare is taught in today’s schools. To redress this omission, parents should turn to Ken Ludwig’s excellent How to Teach Your Children Shakespeare
